Commuting to College

Higher education in Leinster · accessibility, cost, emissions and choice

Commuting to College

Professor John G. Keating, Associate Dean for Teaching & Learning, Faculty of Science & Engineering, Maynooth University. Built with Claude Code assistance (how).

This is individual research and analysis. The views, interpretations and any errors are my own; it is not an official Maynooth University publication and does not represent the University’s position. About this analysis.

How long, how costly and how carbon-heavy is the daily journey from home to college for the young people of Leinster, and does it shape where they choose to study? The study models a weekday commute from every one of Electoral Divisions in 15 counties to 14 higher-education campuses, by public transport and by car, for the people aged 17 to 19 who live there.

From home to every campus

Type the name of a town or Electoral Division. You get the morning journey to each of the 14 campuses by public transport and by car, what a year of that commute costs, and the carbon it emits.

Try:

Morning peak (arrive about 08:30), one representative term Wednesday. Public transport includes the option of driving to a railway station. Costs are for 140 commuting days: student and Young Adult fares (January fare levels) or car fuel plus campus parking and tolls. Carbon is operational CO2 for a single-occupant petrol car or the public-transport mode used; the carbon branch lets you change these assumptions. An Electoral Division is a small statistical area; the figures are for its population-weighted centre.

Methods, data and how to cite

How this was done

Every figure in this report is regenerated by a numbered pipeline of scripts from dated copies of public data. This section sets out the whole method in the order the work was done, then what the results can and cannot support, where the data came from, and how to reproduce it.

About this analysis

Who. John G. Keating, Professor and Associate Dean for Teaching and Learning, Faculty of Science and Engineering, Maynooth University (ORCID 0000-0002-5063-2773).

Status. This is individual research and analysis. The questions, interpretations and any errors are my own. It is not an official Maynooth University publication, it was not commissioned by the University, and it does not represent the University's position or policy.

Funding. This work received no funding.

Why. The daily journey to college shapes who can study where, what it costs families, and what it adds to transport emissions, yet it is rarely measured campus by campus across a whole region. Every input here is public, so the same questions can be asked of any campus, and the answers checked by anyone.

An interest to declare. I work at Maynooth University, one of the fourteen campuses in the study, and Maynooth is the worked example. Every campus is modelled with the same data and the same methods, every tool works for any of them, and the report states plainly where Maynooth comes out poorly: far fewer young people can reach it within an hour by public transport (42%) than by car (69%), and it recruits fewer students than its commute predicts from some of the counties on its doorstep.

How AI was used. The study was built with Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant, working under my direction. It wrote most of the data-processing and modelling code and drafted much of the report's text. I set the questions, made the analytical choices and reviewed the results. Every figure in the report is computed by the published scripts from the published data; none is supplied by the AI. Two kinds of check guard against errors: every number in the report was checked against the output tables before release (that check found and corrected a fault in the enrolment model, recorded in the version history), and the travel-time model is compared with the journeys students report in Census 2022. The code, data and checks are all released so that anyone can repeat them.

Corrections. If you find an error, please open an issue on the repository or email john.keating@mu.ie. Corrections are made in a new version, listed in the version history, and each version keeps its own DOI, so earlier citations remain valid.
